title: SocketCAN: Treat non-CAN-XL packets with length > 16 bytes as CAN-FD
description:
See the reasoning in the code comment.

As we're here, we can also discuss the fact that `PACKET_TYPE_UNKNOWN` is treated exactly the same as `PACKET_TYPE_CAN`. This includes too short or too long CAN-XL frames. Maybe we should simply stop dissecting the packet in that case?

Fix #20328

notes.body: approved this merge request

> The only problem arises when you replay a pcap file from before the cleanup where the CAN FD frame has no FDF set.

> Recent pcap files have the FDF set
>
> Btw. the CAN FD frame from the referenced canfd_frame.pcapng was created 2022-02-17T11:48:43.406032000+0100. So this was an old pcapng file.

Wireshark's goal is not to support what's relevant today, but also what was relevant in the past. We can't ignore the fact that for a long time libraries were writing SocketCAN frames wrong. And also I wouldn't consider 2022 "old".

Currently, Wireshark detects fine any SocketCAN frame that has the correct flags set.

Then, in addition, we try to detect more CAN-FD frames when it's obvious from the size that it can't be Classical CAN. I don't see why this should be a problem.

Sure, it's not perfect, but it can't be.

> So it does not really FIX things but it hides the problem, when the data length is luckily greater than 8 ;-)

I think you're misassuming the role of Wireshark here. The role of the library is to properly set the flags; our role is to make sure we cover all "correct" cases, and try to cover as many deviations from the norm as possible.

Maybe what we can do is to add an expert info when we heuristically detect CAN-FD without the corresponding flag set.

> Then, in addition, we try to detect more CAN-FD frames when it's obvious from the size that it can't be Classical CAN. I don't see why this should be a problem. Sure, it's not perfect, but it can't be.

No. Your heuristic is simply wrong.

The history looks like this:
First we had only Classical CAN (CC). Then CAN FD was invented and the structure size increased from 16 (CAN CC) to 72 (CAN FD) which was the only way to distinguish CAN CC from CAN FD.
In that time I was working towards a proper differentiation with the ETH_P types and everything was fine. Then people started with "unpadded" CAN frames which loses the 16/72 length differentiation without(!) introducing a proper new frame type identifier (FDF). So that all turned into a big mess.

Today the proper identifications are supported either from Wireshark and Libpcap:
- Length identification (16/72)
- FDF to distinguish CAN CC from CAN FD

You now want to create a heuristic that wrongly makes CAN FD frames with <= 8 bytes a CAN CC frame to process pcapng files that have been created in a phase where the CAN support was definitely broken.

If you can not get the information from those pcapng files whether it was a CAN CC frame or a CAN FD frame then this information is LOST. Adding a heuristic over the data length does not fix anything but introduces a bug.

> You now want to create a heuristic that wrongly makes CAN FD frames with <= 8 bytes a CAN CC frame to process pcapng files that have been created in a phase where the CAN support was definitely broken.

The code **already did this before this change. Before this change, CAN FD frames with <= 8 bytes were treated as a CAN CC frame.** !14946 is the change that introduced the heuristic that all frames with <= 8 bytes of data payload without the FDF bit set would be treated as CAN CC, even if actually CAN FD. (As opposed to leaving them as unknown.)

If that's a buggy heuristic, then it's one that you introduced, @hartkopp, and reverting this MR wouldn't change that. So I don't understand your comment.

Before !14946, frames with exactly 8 bytes of data payload were called CAN CC, but those with less were `CAN_TYPE_UNKNOWN` (which may end up being treated as CAN CC). After that change, all frames with less than 8 bytes of data payload were definitively called CAN CC.

> Ehm, no. You probably got that code wrong.
> 
> ```
>             /* CAN CC/FD */
>             if ((tvb_reported_length(tvb) == 72) || (canfd_flags & CANFD_FDF)) {
>                 /* CAN FD: check for min/max data length */
>                 if ((tvb_reported_length(tvb) >= 8) && (tvb_reported_length(tvb) <= 72))
>                     can_packet_type = PACKET_TYPE_CAN_FD;
>             } else if ((tvb_reported_length(tvb) >= 8) && (tvb_reported_length(tvb) <= 16))
>                 can_packet_type = PACKET_TYPE_CAN;
> ```

Imagine two CAN-FD packets with 4 bytes of payload. Packet 1 has the FDF flag set, and packet 2 doesn't.

Can you please tell me what the value of `can_packet_type` would be for both packets, before and after this MR?

This depends on the question if the CAN frame is "unpadded" or not.
Padded CAN frames have a tvb_reported_length() of 16 (CAN CC) or 72 (CAN FD).

E.g. your example in the canfd_frame.pcapng file has a tvb_reported_length() of 40.
Which is an "unpadded" CAN frame with 32 byte of data.

An unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload would have a tvb_reported_length() of 12.

So your check `if ((canfd_flags & CANFD_FDF) || tvb_reported_length(tvb) > 16)` would not be true and such a "CAN FD" frame would be detected as a CAN CC frame. And this is the newly introduced bug with this MR.

The problem emerged with the "unpadded" CAN frames. The CAN data length is simply not a valid identification for CC/FD.
And what does the previous code do with an unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload?

> An unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload would have a tvb_reported_length() of 12.

> When we entered this section (e.g. via CANFD_FDF condition) the possible data lengths from 0 to 64 are ensured. And if this is not the case, this was not a valid CAN FD frame that should be dropped.

OK, but with your code there, if your CANFD_FDF condition is not satisfied, you don't drop it, you proceed to checking

`else if ((tvb_reported_length(tvb) >= 8) && (tvb_reported_length(tvb) <= 16))`

which is true, and set

`can_packet_type = PACKET_TYPE_CAN;`

So we can clearly see that with your code an unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload would have a tvb_reported_length() of 12 gets set to `can_packet_type = PACKET_TYPE_CAN;`.

So as I said, @hartkopp, you are the one who introduced setting `can_packet_type = PACKET_TYPE_CAN` for an unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload and a tvb_reported_length() of 12. Please carefully read your own code.

Unpadded "CAN FD" frames without FDF can not be detected as CAN FD frames.
Therefore we check for the padding (72) and for the FDF flag.

Without FDF we can check only for a correct CAN CC frame which has 0 to 8 CAN data bytes:
```
} else if ((tvb_reported_length(tvb) >= 8) && (tvb_reported_length(tvb) <= 16))
                can_packet_type = PACKET_TYPE_CAN;
```

> Without FDF we can check only for a correct CAN CC frame which has 0 to 8 CAN data bytes:

But an unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload will thus by that code be identified as a "correct CAN CC frame," yes?

An unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload is binary identical with an unpadded CAN CC frame with 4 bytes!
This is the problem when unpadded CAN frames have been introduced. That was not my choice/fault.

So you can only detect CAN FD frames when the `((tvb_reported_length(tvb) == 72) || (canfd_flags & CANFD_FDF))`, right?

> An unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload is binary identical with an unpadded CAN CC frame with 4 bytes! This is the problem when unpadded CAN frames have been introduced. That was not my choice/fault.

You say this.

> So your check `if ((canfd_flags & CANFD_FDF) || tvb_reported_length(tvb) > 16)` would not be true and such a "CAN FD" frame would be detected as a CAN CC frame. **And this is the newly introduced bug with this MR.**

But also this.

Please make up your mind.

Giovanni, please don't get ad hominem!

If you find any reference that I ever introduced unpadded CAN frames or that I ever stated this to be a good idea I will spend you a beer if we meet in real world. This unpadded stuff always caused issues when CAN FD was introduced.

You are taking the CAN data byte length for CC/FD differentiation which is just bogus.

What if people forge a CAN CC frame with a wrong CAN data length greater than 8? Then you make it a CAN FD frame.

The problem is that you have a pcapng file that has been created with an underspecified file format.
You simply can not retrieve the CC/FD status from the CAN data length.

Maybe you use the old setup from 2022 to process the old pcapng files or you might think about some pre-processing or conversion of that old file.

> An unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload is binary identical with an unpadded CAN CC frame with 4 bytes!
This is the problem when unpadded CAN frames have been introduced. That was not my choice/fault.

Yes, it's not your fault that they're indistinguishable, but you are the one who introduced setting them as `PACKET_TYPE_CAN` instead of leaving them as `PACKET_TYPE_UNKNOWN`. That is a reasonable heuristic, but please don't wrongly ascribe this behavior change to this MR as opposed to yours. If you think it's a terrible heuristic, fine, (I think it's reasonable in an impossible situation) but it's yours and don't blame others.

> So you can only detect CAN FD frames when the ((tvb_reported_length(tvb) == 72) || (canfd_flags & CANFD_FDF)), right?

Well, in this case at least the frames with data payload greater than 8 bytes can only legally be CAN FD frames. Yes, someone could forge a bogus frame, but (unlike in the zero to 8 data payload case), it's a very reasonable assumption to treat them as CAN FD. That's especially true since PACKET_TYPE_UNKNOWN implicitly dissects the bytes as CAN CC anyway.

The change from *this* MR is a heuristic that is correct on all but bogus frames. The change in MR !14946 is a reasonable heuristic, but suffers because legitimate CAN CC and CAN FD frames can both have 0 to 8 data payload bytes (so without padding they are indistinguishable.)

All @giovanni.musto did for the 0 to 8 data payload types was add an explanatory comment explicitly pointing out the unavoidable drawbacks in an assumption that was already made by the heuristic in place before this change.

> What if people forge a CAN CC frame with a wrong CAN data length greater than 8? Then you make it a CAN FD frame.

Sure, but what if people forge a CAN CC frame and incorrectly set the FDF bit? Seems as likely.
Btw. this would be a proper CAN FD frame then. The problem shows up when FDF is not set.
Why would that be a "proper CAN FD frame" if it was a CAN CC frame with the FDF bit incorrectly set (but had other traits unique to CAN CC frames)?

@johnthacker please revert this MR.

The latest code from libpcap and Wireshark was the most correct we can provide given the weird history of CAN support in Wireshark. Before the MR the things were cleaned up and only checked for correct identifiers of the different frame types.

The length information in unpadded CAN frames are no proper indicators for CAN CC/FD. And therefore this has nothing to do in any heuristic.

Unfortunately this leads to the problem that some broken(!) unpadded pcapng files can not be processed correctly. But this is no justification to make the implementation worse with introducing a patch which does not entirely fix the problem.

> Giovanni, please don't get ad hominem!

I'm not getting personal. It's just that after all this discussion, it's not yet clear what exactly the problem is.

The only thing that is clear is that you desperately want this MR to be reverted.

If there's a regression, please provide a capture file showing that.

> The only thing that is clear is that you desperately want this MR to be reverted.

It doesn't make things better but introduces an heuristic based on wrong assumptions.
And yes - that makes me desperate when patches are committed that do not consider the whole picture of what is going on and the history of the CAN support of Wireshark.

> If there's a regression, please provide a capture file showing that.

Your pcapng file shows the regression. It shows that 2022 recorded capture files (edit: with unpadded content) lack a proper indication for CAN CC/FD. But this can not be solved by your fix.

It is fixed today (before your patch). And 2022 capture files stay with the problem.

> It doesn't make things better but introduces an heuristic based on wrong assumptions

The heuristic you're complaining about - "An unpadded CAN FD Frame (without FDF) with 4 bytes of payload would have a tvb_reported_length() of 12, and such a "CAN FD" frame would be detected as a CAN CC frame" - was not introduced by this MR. It was introduced by !14946, your change.

I do not see the point in reverting this change. Do you want me to revert !14946? That is what it seems like you are asking for.

> It is fixed today (before your patch).

Without this MR, but with !14946, the code absolutely uses the length information in unpadded CAN frames as an indicator for CAN CC/FD. !14946 decided that all unpadded CAN frames with between 0 and 8 bytes of data payload (and the FDF bit clear) are CAN CC and not CAN FD. Unpadded CAN frames with between 9 and 63 bytes of payload (and the FDF bit cleared) were called Unknown, which is in practice dissected as CAN CC.

> The latest code from libpcap and Wireshark was the most correct we can provide given the weird history of CAN support in Wireshark.

With all due respect, I cannot see this as anything other than completely false. Given an unpadded CAN frame with between 9 and 63 bytes of data payload and the FDF bit clear, it seems enormously more likely that it is a buggy CAN FD frame (given the unfortunate history of many CAN encapsulation producing files) than it is a bogus CAN CC frame with more than the maximum amount of data payload allowed in CAN CC. The former have clearly been produced many times.

It is, again, true that there's no good way to distinguish unpadded frames with between 0 and 8 bytes of data payload - **but the treatment of those frames is entirely unchanged from !14946**

I do not blame you, of course, for the ambiguity caused by incorrect unpadded implementations that do not set the FDF bit. But I seem no possible conceivable reason to revert this MR unless also reverting !14946. If doing anything, it would make more sense to keep the changes here for unpadded data payloads between 9 and 63 (which are unambiguous in all actual implementations) as opposed to your changes in !14946 for unpadded data payloads between 0 and 7 (which are, as you agree, unfortunately ambiguous in known real world implementations.)

What could, I think, be some reasonable alternatives:

1. Add expert info indicators for frames which clearly have data payload in the CAN FD range but lack the FDF bit set - whether they're treated as CAN CC or CAN FD or something in between, that's clearly bogus and should be indicated.
2. Add expert info indicators and appropriate handling for ambiguous frames that are left in a `PACKET_TYPE_UNKNOWN` - right now those are dissected as though they are CAN CC, which means that if you choose not to decide on the packet type, you have effectively still chosen CAN CC, which is much less likely to be the correct choice in the large payload case but perhaps more likely than not in the small payload case.

Or any number of options.

It is very clear to me from the discussion in the other MR that the result *after* this MR is closer to what was requested in the comments.

> without requiring all CAN FD frames to have an "original length" of 72 (8+64) octets and requiring all CAN CC frames to have an "original length" of 16 (8+8) octets,

Before this MR, all CAN FD frames were required to either have the FDF bit set or have an original length of 72. *No* unpadded CAN FD frames without the FDF bit set (a case clearly abundantly present in real life, unlike CAN CC frames with greater than 8 bytes of data payload) would work.

Can you please explain your reasoning? Is it that you feel that a single capture should not be treated as having a mix of CAN FD and CAN CC frames, depending on the unpadded data payload length of individual frames, and that it would be better for all the frames to be incorrectly treated as CAN CC rather than any (most) of them treated correctly?

@johnthacker I have been working as maintainer of the Linux CAN Subsystem for more than 16 years now.
Most of the CAN-related Wireshark/libpcap code and changes are from @guyharris and most of my discussions have been done together with @guyharris which I would like to invite here and clarify the issue with this MR.
Using the data byte length to separate Classical CAN from CAN FD frames is simply WRONG. And therefore adding such "by-length-identification" into the heuristic is also WRONG.

Maybe @guyharris has some idea how to restore the CAN FD information/identification from the referenced 2022 pcapng file as he is working on both sides on the DLT_CAN_SOCKETCAN implementation.

The patch from this MR only makes unpadded CAN frames with a data length > 8 a CAN FD frame. CAN FD frames with a data length <= 8 remain Classical CAN frames. This is just a "works-for-me-hack" for unpadded 2022 capture files where only "longer-than-8" data bytes CAN FD frames are recorded in the capture file. Seriously a bad hack.

You ask if treating "some" CAN FD frames (with a data length > 8) "correctly" as CAN FD is better than treating them all as CAN CC? No it is not, because the CAN FD frames (with a data length <= 8) are then treated wrongly.
With the patch it "feels" better (only) for some cases but it hides the problem from the 2022 capture file.
Therefore it is better that people see that things go wrong instead of getting definitely unreliable content. I hope you see that the same way.

> Therefore it is better that people see that things go wrong instead of getting definitely unreliable content. I hope you see that the same way.

I argue it is not. It is not the purpose of Wireshark to "educate" the user, nor the library developer. Wireshark has to support correctly formed packets, but also try its best with malformed packets (if this does not cause issues with well-formed packets).

If you take a look at any other dissector, you will find similar stuff in there. This is because in the real world, you don't always find perfect implementations. Sometimes developers (i.e. people) get it wrong, and some errors persist for a long time. Sometimes they persist for so long they become de-facto standards. And we can't ignore that.

I think, speaking in general terms, it should be Wireshark's goal to support as much as possible, as long as it doesn't cause side effects. This is especially true because Wireshark opens offline logs, that could have been captured anytime in the past.

Your argument is that, since the heuristic doesn't work for payload lengths between 0 and 8, it should be removed entirely, even if it works just fine for lengths between 9 and 64, without having any side effects on correctly formed frames. I just can't get why.

What we can do, as already suggested, is to add an expert info, so that the user knows the frame does not perfectly adhere to the SocketCAN specification. But, in my opinion, it doesn't make sense to revert the MR entirely.

It now seems that you are desperately want this MR to be approved.

The vital purpose for every tool is to work correctly and not to make the user feel good or create truth for uncertain input data.

> Wireshark has to support correctly formed packets, but also try its best with malformed packets (if this does not cause issues with well-formed packets).

Try its best until the heuristic comes to the point that it knowingly lies. And you know that CAN FD frames with a data length of 0 .. 8 are detected as CAN CC frames. In this case you approve the obviously under-specified content to be CAN CC.

> Your argument is that, since the heuristic doesn't work for payload lengths between 0 and 8, it should be removed entirely, even if it works just fine for lengths between 9 and 64, without having any side effects on correctly formed frames. I just can't get why.

The patch tries to obtain the missing FDF flag from the unpadded data byte length. This is simply not doable.
For CAN FD frames with a length 0 .. 8 your heuristic is always 100% wrong.

Instead of creating wrong results from under-specified content it is better to do nothing, so that the user can detect the problem and has the ability to react accordingly.

Consider the following table for unpadded CAN frames (properly padded frames, including CAN FD frames padded to 72 with the FDF bit clear, work fine in all cases):

| |Before !14946 | Post !14946 | Post !18710 | Likely true value
| ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ | ----- |
| FDF 0, Data 0-7 | UNKNOWN | CAN CC | CAN CC | **UNDERSPECIFIED**
| FDF 0, Data 9-63| UNKNOWN | UNKNOWN| CAN FD | CAN FD
| FDF 1, Data 0-63| UNKNOWN | CAN FD | CAN FD | CAN FD

This table elides over the fact that in practice, the dissector treats UNKNOWN as CAN CC, not CAN FD; that could be addressed separately.

> Try its best until the heuristic comes to the point that it knowingly lies. And you know that CAN FD frames with a data length of 0 .. 8 are detected as CAN CC frames. In this case you approve the obviously under-specified content to be CAN CC.

The underspecified case is the first row. The MR that caused CAN FD frames with a data length of 0 .. 8 to be detected as CAN CC frames is !14946. It is !14946 that approves the obviously underspecified content to be CAN CC. That has nothing to do with this MR.

> The patch tries to obtain the missing FDF flag from the unpadded data byte length. This is simply not doable. For CAN FD frames with a length 0 .. 8 your heuristic is always 100% wrong.

It is !14946 that introduced the heuristic of being always 100% wrong for CAN FD frames with a missing FDF flags and length 0 .. 7. (Unpadded CAN FD frames with a length of 8 and missing the FDF flag were always wrong, because that is the padded CAN CC length.)

> Instead of creating wrong results from under-specified content it is better to do nothing, so that the user can detect the problem and has the ability to react accordingly.

So clearly you are asking me to revert or partially revert your !14946, @hartkopp?

> Therefore it is better that people see that things go wrong instead of getting definitely unreliable content.

Thank you for explaining your position more in that sentence. So the strongest version of your argument that I can make is:

"A capture consisting of unpadded CAN CC frames (naturally with the FDF bit clear) can be made to work 100%, so it is OK to approve all the frames as being CAN CC, even if that is under-specified and could be confused with unpadded CAN FD frames with the FDF bit clear that happen to be short. We can, by deciding that all the frames are CAN CC, guarantee that we correctly process all the frames in the capture. We should allow this particular type of (buggy, pre 2022 capture) to be processed without warning the user, and hide the problem, because it works for CAN CC. 2022 and earlier captures that do this can be dissected fine.

A capture consisting of unpadded CAN FD frames with the FDF bit clear is *more* wrong than a capture of unpadded CAN CC frames with the FDF bit clear or unpadded CAN FD frames with the FDF bit set. It's making two mistakes. What's more, such a capture can contain some frames that have length 0-8 and some frames that are 9-64. We cannot guarantee that all the frames in the capture are correctly processed with a simple heuristic. Faced with such a capture, there's a good chance that we will have some frames correctly processed as CAN FD and some incorrectly processed as CAN CC. That is worse than the CAN CC case above; it is so bad, that we would rather have the short frames determined to definitely be CAN CC and the long frames left UNKNOWN (but in practice treated as CAN CC). This by itself should be obvious enough that things have gone wrong that people will fix their tools. We shouldn't care about people being able to dissect their 2022 and earlier captures as well as possible, only that they use the right tools going forward."

I personally think rather it would make more sense to warn with an expert info in *all* cases of unpadded unambiguous frames and all cases of "only legal for CAN FD length but the FDF bit is clear" frames. It might also make sense to have a preference to make it possible for someone to override the heuristic and "yes, I know I am dissecting a buggy 2022 unpadded CAN FD capture with the FDF bit clear, please dissect frames of length 0-8 as CAN FD as well" - this would not be the default setting.

[canfd_frame_WS36.pcapng](/uploads/4f3c926af8f7ea2b61f2500b76d7e6c6/canfd_frame_WS36.pcapng)

I got my old Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS Laptop with Wireshark 3.6.2 (libpcap 1.10.1) and created some random CAN CC/FD traffic. The capture file is attached. And it works great with the latest Wireshark - without this MR patch we are discussing about.

It looks like that WS 3.6.2 creates padded pcapng files which is good.
@giovanni.musto 's pcapng file shows a CAN CC(!!) frame with 32 bytes data length in WS 3.6.2 !

After WS 3.6.2 something broke the pcapng format with introducing unpadded content without adding the FDF flag.
The unpadded capture files that have been created in that phase are simply broken, or do you have a Wireshark version, that replays your file correctly @giovanni.musto ??

I always show up in the Wireshark/libpcap development when I see, that tings are broken or when new features (like CAN XL) can be integrated. But we simply can not fix the capture files from a period where the pcapng file generation was broken.

The canfd_frame.pcapng file is broken in WS3.6.2 and in the latest WS master branch. Just broken.

Today everything is fixed, cleaned up and simplified and even old WS3.6.2 capture files are working properly. Thanks, Oliver!

And now @giovanni.musto shows up with a broken capture file and wants to break the repaired code with a broken heuristic depending on the unsuitable data length information.

Therefore this MR has to be reverted. You destroy the 100% correct code in favor of a broken capture file which additionally creates wrong content for CAN FD frames with <= 8 bytes of data length.

Sorry for the broken canfd_frame.pcapng capture file. It was not my fault. But it can not be fixed within Wireshark.

[canfd_frame_WS36_Kernel515.pcapng](/uploads/0ba2d990ae92ef63b1017cca14406fd7/canfd_frame_WS36_Kernel515.pcapng)

The former pcapng file was created with WS 3.6.2 Ubuntu 22.04 and Kernel 6.1 - which always has the FDF bit set.

This pcapng file was captured with the original Ubuntu 22.04 Linux 5.15 Kernel, where the FDF bit was not set by the kernel. But as the capture file is padded the CAN CC/FD separation is still correct in WS 3.6.2 and the latest WS.

> And it works great with the latest Wireshark - without this MR patch we are discussing about.

It also works with this MR, as does the other pcap. So that is not at all an argument for reverting the patch.

> Therefore this MR has to be reverted. You destroy the 100% correct code

You haven't demonstrated a single file which is handled worse with this code. You have demonstrated that some broken files are handled better with this code.

AFAICT, you think that handling doubly broken files slightly better is "destroying 100% correct code", even if no file whatsoever is handled worse and some are handled better. I certainly would not want to try to handle broken files better in a way that would at all worsen the handling of more correct files, but you agree that's not happening here. There are no correct files, nor even files that are broken but only on one dimension instead of two (and thus less broken) that are treated worse by this code.

The only argument I can see you have made is that you would rather broken files be treated entirely as CAN CC even for frames where that is almost surely incorrect.

With absolutely no personal animus intended, your arguments are unpersuasive at best and self-contradictory at worst. You are arguing to make the code worse for no apparent benefit, just breaking things with not even the barest hint of justification, even when I attempted to offer you one you reject it.

> even if no file whatsoever is handled worse and some are handled better.

No, this is not true. Why are you always stating, that the MR has no drawbacks?
When you have an unpadded CAN FD frame without FDF and a data byte length <= 8 then this frame is detected as CAN CC frame which is wrong. Using the data length information for CAN CC/FD differentiation is wrong. Introducing code that uses the data length information for such reason is therefore wrong.

There is no micro improvement you like to see.

Another thing that should really be fixed, is that the entire packet should be dropped when we don't detect a proper CAN frame and the can_packet_type remains PACKET_TYPE_UNKNOWN. Defaulting this to CAN CC is wrong. I wasn't aware of that issue before you pointed it out ...

> When you have an unpadded CAN FD frame without FDF and a data byte length \<= 8 then this frame is detected as CAN CC frame which is wrong.

Once again, as stated multiple times before, this was already the case before.

**It is not this MR that introduced this change.**

In other words, reverting this MR will make absolutely no difference for **unpadded CAN FD frame without FDF and a data byte length \<= 8**. They were detected as CAN CC before, and they are detected as CAN CC now.

**Before going on, do we agree at least on this?**

Given the answer to the previous question is yes, as we agreed before, there's no way to differentiate an **unpadded CAN FD frame without FDF and a data byte length \<= 8** from a **CAN CC frame a data byte length \<= 8**.

We can either:
1. Accept the fact that the two are indistinguishable, and accept the fact that the heuristic works in all cases, except this one, and it's not our fault.
2. Disallow unpadded frames entirely and only accept lengths of 16 or 72. Frames with other lengths are ignored and the FDF flag is used to further confirm the nature of the frame.

Let's suppose we chose option 2 and we see a SocketCAN frame with length 16 and FDF bit clear. Is this a correctly formed CAN CC frame, or an unpadded CAN-FD frame of length 8 without the FDF bit set?

**We can't know, because they are indistinguishable! Even the most strict of the rules will interpret it as CAN CC!**

If you're in the kernel, you can count on the fixed length of the frame, because it comes from the size of the `struct`, but you can not do the same in the field, where frames are stored unpadded, and the FDF bit is not always used. We WILL encounter such a packet in the wild, and even the most strict of the heuristic (option 2) will fail in that case.

You could say "but they are indistinguishable, it is correct to treat them as CAN CC". Fine. Then why do we need option 2 if the same result is already achieved now, and was already achieved before? Why exclude frames that are perfectly valid, if not for the fact that they are unpadded?

At this point I (ironically) suggest removing CAN-FD support entirely from Wireshark since it cannot work 100% of the time.

So here's [the current tcpdump.org description of the `LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN` pseudo-header](https://www.tcpdump.org/linktypes/LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN.html). It says (or will say, once some fixes I committed get propagated to the web site): > This format supports CAN CC (classic CAN), CAN FD, and CAN XL frames. > The same header is used for CAN CC and CAN FD frames; a different header > is used for CAN XL frames. > > The `0x80` bit of the fifth octet of the header is clear for > CAN CC and CAN FD frames, and set for CAN XL frames. > > ### CAN CC and CAN FD frames > > #### Packet structure > > ``` > +---------------------------+ > | CAN ID and flags | > | (4 Octets) | > +---------------------------+ > | Payload length | > | (1 Octet) | > +---------------------------+ > | FD flags | > | (1 Octet) | > +---------------------------+ > | Reserved/Padding | > | (1 Octet) | > +---------------------------+ > | Reserved/Padding | > | (1 Octet) | > +---------------------------+ > | Payload | > . . > . . > . . > +---------------------------+ > | Padding | > . . > . . > . . > ``` > > #### Description> > > The CAN ID and flags field is in network byte order (big-endian). > The bottom 29 bits contain the CAN ID of the frame. > The remaining bits are: > > * `0x20000000` - set if the frame is an error message rather than a data frame. > * `0x40000000` - set if the frame is a remote transmission request frame. > * `0x80000000` - set if the frame is an extended 29-bit frame rather than a standard 11-bit frame. > > The frame payload length indicates the number of bytes of payload > following the header. All packet bytes after those bytes of payload are > padding. > > The FD flags field contains CAN FD specific flags; for CAN CC frames, > this field is 0. The bits are: > > * `CANFD_BRS` (`0x01`) - bit rate switch (second bitrate for payload data). > * `CANFD_ESI` (`0x02`) - error state indicator of the transmitting node. > * `CANFD_FDF` (`0x04`) - if set, the frame is a CAN FD frame; if not set, > the frame may be a CAN CC frame or a CAN FD frame. > > Older software and firmware writing packets with this link type did not > use the `CANFD_FDF` flag for CAN FD frames, so if the > `CANFD_FDF` flag is not set, the frame is not guaranteed to > be a CAN CC frame. If that flag is not set: > > * if the frame size (including the header and padding) is 16, it's > a CAN CC frame; > * if the frame size (including the header and padding) is 72, it's > a CAN FD frame. > > In addition, older software and firmware may not have explicitly set > that field, so that the bit corresponding to the `CANFD_FDF` > flag might be set even for CAN CC frames. Therefore, code that reads > `LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN` frames must perform some heuristic > checks to make sure that it doesn't incorrectly interpret a CAN CC frame > as a CAN FD frame, and code that generates > `LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN` frames must follow certain rules to > make sure that those checks don't cause software that reads those fromes > to treat a CAN FD frame as a CAN CC frame. > > Software that reads `LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN` frames must not > treat a frame with the `CANFD_FDF` bit set as a CAN FD frame > if any bits other than `CANFD_BRS` and `CANFD_ESI` > are set in that field, or if either of the Reserved/Padding fields are > non-zero, as that is an indication that the header fields might not have > been explicitly set, and the `CANFD_FDF` flag might happen to > be set even thugh the frame is not a CAN FD frame. > > Software that generates `LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN` frames: > > * Must check the frame MTU when receiving frames from the Linux > kernel in order to classify them as CAN CC frames or CAN FD frames. > * Must make the "FD flags" field 0 for CAN CC frames. > * Must set the `CANFD_FDF` bit of the "FD flags" field in CAN FD frames, > and don't set any bits in that field other than the `CANFD_BRS` and `CANFD_ESI` bits > unless and until Linux assigns them a meaning. > * Must make the "Reserved/Padding" fields 0 unless and until Linux assigns > that particular field a meaning. > * May strip trailing padding bytes to save disk space if all above statements are satisfied. > > For a data frame, the payload is the data field of the CAN CC or CAN FD > packet. > > For a remote retransmission request, the payload length must be 0, so > the payload is empty. > > For an error message, the payload is always 8 bytes. The lower bits of > the CAN ID field contain an error class value, with bits specified by > the first set of `CAN_ERR_` values in href="https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/include/uapi/linux/can/error.h">the > Linux `uapi/can/error.h` header. The bytes in the payload are: > > * first byte - if arbitration was lost, the bit number in the bitstream in which it was lost; > otherwise 0. > * second byte - the error status of the CAN controller, with bits > specified by the `CAN_ERR_CRTL_` bits in the Linux `uapi/can/error.h` > header. > * third byte - flags indicating a CAN protocol error type, with bits > specified by the `CAN_ERR_PROT_` bits in the Linux `uapi/can/error.h` > header. > * fourth byte - flags indicating a CAN protocol error location, with > bits specified by the `CAN_ERR_LOC_` bits in the Linux `uapi/can/error.h` > header. > * fifth byte - the error status of the CAN transceiver, with values > specified by the `CAN_ERR_TRX_` values in the Linux `uapi/can/error.h` > header. > * sixth, seventh, and eighth bytes - controller-specific additional > information. > > ### CAN XL frames > > #### Packet structure> > > ``` > +---------------------------+ > | Priority ID/VCID | > | (4 Octets) | > +---------------------------+ > | Flags | > | (1 Octet) | > +---------------------------+ > | SDU type | > | (1 Octet) | > +---------------------------+ > | Payload length | > | (2 Octets) | > +---------------------------+ > | Acceptance Field | > | (4 Octets) | > +---------------------------+ > | Payload | > . . > . . > . . > +---------------------------+ > | Padding | > . . > . . > . . > ``` > > #### Description> > > *The Priority ID/VCID field is big-endian, but the payload length and > acceptance field are little-endian.* > > The Priority ID/VCID field is in big-endian byte order. > The bottom 11 bits contain the priority of the frame. The 5 bits above > that are reserved. The 8 bits above that contain a virtual CAN > network identifier (VCID). The 8 bits above that are reserved. > > The flags field contains CAN XL specific flags. The bits are: > > * `CANFD_SEC` (`0x01`) - Simple Extended Context. > * `CANXL_XLF` (`0x80`) - if set, the frame is a CAN XL frame; if not set, > the frame is a CAN CC frame or a CAN FD frame. > > The SDU type field contains an indication of the higher-layer protocol > used by the payload. The values of this field are specified by CAN in > Automation (CiA) specification 611-1 "CAN XL higher-layer functions - > Part 1: Definition of service data unit types (SDT)". > > The frame payload length is in little-endian byte order. > It indicates the number of bytes of payload > following the header. All packet bytes after those bytes of payload are > padding. > > The Acceptance Field is in little-endian byte order. So those are what are documented as the rules for handling both valid and old-and-invalid CAN frames. If there are any errors, please file an issue on [the tcpdump.org web site's issue list](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/tcpdump-htdocs/issues), or file a pull request on [that site's pull request list](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/tcpdump-htdocs/pulls).

And here's [a comment on a previous pull request from Oliver](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/tcpdump-htdocs/pull/37#discussion_r1554325088), concerning the "what do we do about `CAN_FDF`" issue:

> Note that, currently, Wireshark handles non-pcap/pcapng CAN capture files, such as Vector Informatik BLF files, [BUSMASTER](https://rbei-etas.github.io/busmaster/) files, dumps from Linux candump, and log files from CL*x*000 [CAN loggers from CSS Electronics](https://www.csselectronics.com/pages/can-bus-hardware-products), by constructing a fake SocketCAN header from whatever metadata is available in the native file format and prepending that header to the CAN frame data.
> 
> This means that, if those files were to be read by a program in the Wireshark suite and written out as a pcap or pcapng file, there would be LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN packets without the padding Linux SocketCAN adds.  The frame size check can't be used for those packets; the flags have to be checked 
> 
> Either the spec should allow for that, or the Wireshark code that writes LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN packets should pad CAN CC frames to 16 octets (including the SocketCAN header) and pad CAN FD frames to 72 octets (again, including the SocketCAN header).

@guyharris 
I rebased my PR as requested.
Here is the HTML file for those who want to download and view it in a browser.

https://github.com/hartkopp/tcpdump-htdocs/blob/SocketCAN-DLT-update-2025-rebased/linktypes/LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN.html

> May strip trailing padding bytes to save disk space if all above statements are satisfied.

So yes, I see that unpadded frames with the FDF bit set correctly (clear for CAN CC and set for CAN FD) are valid. That is certainly a good reason to interpret packets with an appropriate length and the FDF bit cleared as CAN CC (even though it could be ambiguous with old buggy implementations, correct implementations should be preferred by default.)

There are currently (either before or are this MR), no checks of the sort "was the FDF bit set by mistake in a CAN CC frames" by checking "if CANFD_BRS and CANFD_ESI are set in that field, or if either of the Reserved/Padding fields are non-zero." There may have been at some point, but currently if the FDF bit is set it is always treated as a CAN FD frame.

Given that some heuristic must be performed, I see little reason to avoid marking frames with a payload too large for CAN CC as CAN FD by default. There could be utility in a preference to override the default heuristic in several ambiguous cases.

> There are currently (either before or are this MR), no checks of the sort "was the FDF bit set by mistake in a CAN CC frames" by checking "if CANFD_BRS and CANFD_ESI are set in that field, or if either of the Reserved/Padding fields are non-zero." There may have been at some point, but currently if the FDF bit is set it is always treated as a CAN FD frame.

Yes. And I doubt that discussing about "accidentally set FDF bits" makes even sense.
The CAN frames you get from the Linux kernel are always zero-initialized correctly to not leak any kernel data to userspace. And the other LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN sources are from the adapters for BUSMASTER, BLF and others that hopefully(?) also create proper initialized content. So for CAN CC/FD differentiation the FDF bit is perfectly fine.
E.g. this libpcap patch https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/pull/1310/commits/9b427394ad60296569732899b1956aeec3ed1dea reduces the sanitizing and only makes sure that the CANXL_XLF and CANFD_FDF bits are valid.

> Given that some heuristic must be performed, I see little reason to avoid marking frames with a payload too large for CAN CC as CAN FD by default.

A CAN CC frame with a CAN data length greater than 8 should be dropped as it is not a valid CAN frame.

Again: Using the CAN data length as a qualifier for CAN FD is wrong.
The 4 bit CAN (CC & FD) Data Length Code (DLC) goes from 0 .. 15. For CAN FD the DLC is mapped non-linear to the 0 .. 64 bytes length information.

- CAN CC has valid DLC values 0 .. 8
- CAN FD has valid DLC values 0 .. 15

As CAN CC has the same value range you have a 9/16 chance that a CAN FD frame is tagged as CAN CC.

It can not be an argument that Giovanni's capture files luckily only have CAN FD frames with a data length of 32 bytes. We have to provide a heuristic that is correct or even best-effort for the entire range of data lengths. And this is not given here.
DLC values 9 to 15 are not illegal in CAN CC, they are simply interpreted as 8 (ISO 11898-1:2015 section 8.4.2.4).

Yes. This was only to show the DLC effect on real the data length value which is discussed here.
I just wanted to point out, that length values > 8 have a 7/16 chance and not 55/64.

So your (hopefully final) argument is that the only allowed frames are:
- Frames with length 8..16 without FDF (interpreted as Classical CAN)
- Frames with length 8..72 with FDF (interpreted as CAN-FD)
- Frames with length 72 without FDF (exception to support pre-2022 CAN-FD)

Any other frame must be discarded.

Is it correct?

Exactly!

The "Frames with length 72 without FDF" is the detection via the (padded) structure length.

This is relevant for CAN FD frames that have been captured from an older Linux kernel that didn't had the CANFD_FDF bit set. Today this bit is set even for captures taken on old kernels inside libpcap:
https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/blob/cf33e7e2aace3c1ceb5e921ebe9a4fe282db19c0/pcap-linux.c#L4122

To catch CAN CC frames via the (padded) structure length your first point already does the job.
I've updated the description of LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN frames to include a bulleted-list version of the algorithm above as the way to determine the frame type for those frames.

Excellent!

I hope the `return tvb_captured_length(tvb);` is the correct way to leave the dissector in these 'drop invalid frame' cases?

When there's no more feedback from @giovanni.musto and @johnthacker I would send a MR with two patches that ...

1. reverts the original patch from this MR discussion
2. add the dropping of invalid frames

... so that the code looks finally like the code above.

Adding the expert info would be a separate step.
